Baby & Child

COVID-19 vaccine side effects in children: what parents should know

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Most reactions to a COVID-19 vaccine are short-lived, but parents should know which symptoms need help. The decision also depends on a child’s health and the current local vaccination guidance, which has changed since the first childhood vaccines were introduced.

Children can catch and pass on COVID-19

Children are not simply smaller adults: their risk of severe disease, vaccine doses and the way they show symptoms can differ. Many infections in children are mild or cause no symptoms, but children can still become seriously ill and can pass SARS-CoV-2 to other people. A child who feels well may still be infectious.

The virus spreads through infectious respiratory particles, particularly in shared indoor air. School and childcare create opportunities for repeated close contact, but a child’s exposure also depends on local circulation, ventilation, activities and household contacts. School attendance alone does not establish that every child has more exposure than every adult.

Who is more likely to become seriously ill?

Serious COVID-19 can involve breathing difficulty, dehydration, hospital admission and, in some cases, intensive care or death. It can happen without a known underlying condition, although risk is not evenly distributed. Infants account for a disproportionate share of severe paediatric cases and hospital assessments; prematurity and the need to investigate fever in young infants also influence hospital figures.

Conditions such as diabetes, obesity, significant heart, lung or neurological disease, immune suppression and complex health needs can increase risk. Sickle cell disease is another condition to discuss with the child’s clinician. These factors concern the risk of a poor outcome as well as, in some circumstances, exposure or susceptibility; they should not all be described simply as making infection more likely.

Persistent symptoms after infection and the uncommon inflammatory illness called MIS-C are also part of the discussion. The child’s own medical history is more useful for decisions than a single average hospitalisation percentage quoted for all children.

Keep early-pandemic statistics in their historical context

The school closures and vaccine trials of 2020 and 2021 explain why many families first encountered this topic. Those figures do not describe the current season. A report saying that children made up a quarter of reported cases meant a share of identified cases, not that one in four children was infected.

US surveillance during the Delta wave in summer 2021 found an approximately fivefold increase in weekly hospitalisation rates among under-18s and an approximately tenfold increase in those aged zero to four between selected weeks. A comparison in adolescents also found substantially higher hospitalisation rates among those unvaccinated at that time. Those were historical observations with specific populations and dates, not permanent multipliers for a child today.

Similarly, the fraction of hospitalised children needing intensive care is not the fraction of all infected children who will need it. Intensive care may provide close monitoring, oxygen, medicines or other support; it does not always mean a ventilator. Variant changes, previous infections, vaccination, testing and admission practices all affect comparisons over time.

Do masks and other school precautions help?

An Arizona study of schools in July and August 2021 found higher adjusted odds of a school-associated outbreak where there was no mask requirement at the start of term. The widely quoted figure of 3.5 referred to the odds of an outbreak in a school, not an individual child being exactly 3.5 times as likely to catch the virus.

It was an observational study from a particular period, so differences between schools and other preventive measures matter. Cleaner indoor air, staying home when acutely unwell and a well-fitting mask when appropriate can form a layered approach. Follow current local and age-appropriate advice, including the needs of children who cannot safely or comfortably wear a mask. Vaccination is one part of protection rather than a guarantee that transmission stops.

Which children can receive a vaccine now?

The original Pfizer authorisations for ages 12 to 15 and 16 and over were milestones in 2021, not the current age limits. Research subsequently included younger children, and formulations and recommendations have changed. A product’s approval, a public-health recommendation and availability in a local programme are separate questions.

As checked on 7 October 2026, US CDC guidance for 2026–27 recommends vaccination for children aged six months to 17 years with moderate or severe immune compromise. For other children in that age range, it recommends shared clinical decision making with a healthcare professional. Product choice and dosing depend on age, previous doses and immune status, and some uses described in the guidance are outside the FDA-approved indication.

Canada’s NACI guidance starting in autumn 2026 prioritises people at higher risk, including children from six months with relevant medical conditions or complex health needs. Programmes may also offer vaccination to others from six months based on individual risk or preference. Other countries can take different approaches. Check the current local schedule with the vaccination service rather than using an old age chart or an adult dose.

What benefits can vaccination offer?

The main aim is to reduce serious illness. Protection against infection and transmission is incomplete and can decline as immunity wanes and the virus changes. The benefit for a particular child depends on underlying risk, prior infection or vaccination, circulating variants and the product offered.

A US study published in December 2025 found that 2024–25 vaccination was associated with fewer COVID-related emergency-department or urgent-care visits in children. That outcome is different from preventing every infection or measuring deaths, and an estimate from one season should not be promised for every later product or age group.

The decision is therefore not made by comparing a mild sore arm with a claim that all childhood COVID is harmless. It weighs a child’s chance of meaningful benefit against common short-term reactions and uncommon serious risks. Vaccination does not by itself guarantee an end to circulation or replace other measures when a family member is particularly vulnerable.

Common reactions after the injection

A sore or tender injection site is common; there may also be redness or swelling. Tiredness, headache, muscle or joint aches, chills and fever can occur. Younger children may instead seem fussy, sleepier, feed less enthusiastically or temporarily lose their appetite. Some children have few or no noticeable reactions.

Most expected reactions are mild to moderate and settle within a few days, commonly one to three days. An exact 48-hour deadline is too rigid. The pattern should generally improve. Symptoms that worsen, persist, or do not fit the expected pattern deserve advice rather than being automatically attributed to the vaccine.

Having no fever or arm soreness does not mean that vaccination failed. Equally, a symptom appearing after vaccination is not automatically caused by it: respiratory infections and other illnesses can happen at the same time. Assess how the child is doing overall, including drinking, breathing and alertness.

Helping a child feel comfortable

Offer fluids, allow rest and use a cool, damp cloth on a sore injection site. Gentle ordinary movement is usually fine if the child feels well. There is no need to force normal activities when they are tired or uncomfortable.

If pain or fever is bothering the child, ask a pharmacist or clinician about an age- and weight-appropriate medicine such as acetaminophen, also called paracetamol, or ibuprofen if suitable. Check the exact product strength and avoid giving multiple products containing the same ingredient. Do not give aspirin to a child unless specifically prescribed.

Routine pain medicine before vaccination is not generally recommended just to prevent symptoms. A child already taking a medicine for another condition should follow their clinician’s advice rather than stopping it without discussion. Seek help for poor drinking, reduced urination, unusual drowsiness, persistent fever or any symptom that concerns you.

Rare heart inflammation: myocarditis and pericarditis

Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle; pericarditis affects the sac around the heart. Both have been reported rarely after COVID-19 vaccination. With mRNA vaccines, reports have been most frequent in adolescent and young adult males, often within a week after a second dose, although other sexes and doses can be affected. Risk varies by age, product, dose and interval.

Seek prompt urgent assessment for new chest pain, shortness of breath or palpitations after vaccination, particularly during the following week. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or severe chest pain requires emergency care. A younger child may show less specific signs such as unusual lethargy, rapid breathing, vomiting or poor feeding.

Many affected patients improve with treatment and rest, but follow-up matters. Improvement in symptoms does not automatically establish that every heart finding has resolved. A clinician should guide recovery and return to strenuous activity rather than a child returning to sport simply because the chest pain has eased.

How to understand the heart-risk numbers

A June 2025 FDA safety update described estimates from the 2023–24 mRNA formulations: approximately eight myocarditis or pericarditis cases per million doses across ages six months to 64 years, and approximately 27 per million in males aged 12 to 24, during days one to seven. These were unadjusted estimates from insurance-claims data, not a risk that applies equally to every child or every current vaccine.

The same update described persistent cardiac MRI abnormalities in some people followed after vaccine-associated myocarditis. Their long-term clinical meaning was uncertain. This supports discussing the risk honestly and taking symptoms seriously without implying that every vaccinated child has hidden heart injury.

COVID-19 infection can also cause cardiac complications. Comparing infection and vaccine risks requires the same age group, outcome definition, time window and other relevant factors. A single early unpublished estimate should not be used as a universal ratio or as a personal prediction. Ask the clinician to explain the relevant evidence for the child and the product being considered.

Severe allergic reactions and other urgent symptoms

Anaphylaxis is a rare severe allergic reaction. Breathing difficulty, swelling of the tongue or throat, widespread hives with other symptoms, or collapse needs immediate emergency treatment. If this happens at the vaccination clinic, alert staff at once; after leaving, call the local emergency number. Antihistamines are not a substitute for emergency care.

Follow the observation period requested by the vaccination team. Tell them in advance about a severe reaction to a previous dose or a known vaccine-component allergy. Fainting around an injection can also occur, especially in adolescents, and is managed differently; staff should assess rather than a parent trying to distinguish serious symptoms alone.

A seizure, severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, inability to wake normally or rapid deterioration warrants emergency help whatever the suspected cause. A rare event listed for one vaccine technology should not automatically be assigned to every COVID-19 product. The current product information and the child’s assessment are the relevant guides.

What if there was a reaction to an earlier dose?

Bring the date, product, symptoms, timing and any medical records to the next discussion. A sore arm or a short fever does not necessarily prevent another dose, while a serious allergic reaction requires a specific assessment. Do not assume all products have identical ingredients or risks.

CDC advises that myocarditis or pericarditis within three weeks of a COVID-19 vaccine is a precaution and that another dose should generally be avoided. Any exception needs an individual specialist risk assessment after recovery. A history of MIS-C or heart inflammation unrelated to a vaccine also needs a clinician-led plan.

Report a suspected important reaction through the local vaccine-safety system or ask the clinician to help. A report is useful for investigation even when causation is uncertain; reports alone are not proof that a vaccine caused every event recorded.

Questions to take to the vaccination appointment

Ask which product is recommended for the child’s age and health, which formulation is being used, whether previous infection or doses affect timing, and whether the use is within local approval. Ask which reactions to expect and whom to contact after hours.

For a child with a chronic condition, immune suppression or a previous serious reaction, ask how that changes the expected benefit and monitoring. You can discuss both the protection offered and the uncertainties without being rushed. Use the current seasonal guidance rather than a screenshot from an earlier pandemic year.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current US 2026–27 and Canadian autumn-2026 guidance were checked; schedules and product approvals remain country- and age-specific.

Common reactions are usually brief. Rare serious reactions require appropriate assessment, and safety estimates must be tied to the product, age group and time period studied.

How BeMama can help

Keep the product and vaccination date with the child’s records and ask for a practical plan for common symptoms and urgent concerns.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, throat swelling, collapse, a seizure or inability to wake normally. New chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations after vaccination needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Children can develop and transmit COVID-19, even when many infections are mild.
  • Use current local eligibility and product advice.
  • Sore arms, tiredness and fever usually settle within a few days.
  • Heart inflammation and severe allergy are rare but need prompt recognition.
  • Historical statistics are not a personal prediction for the current season.

Frequently asked questions

What side effects are most common in children?

A sore injection site, tiredness, headache, aches, chills or fever can occur. Young children may be fussy, sleepy or eat less. Some children have no noticeable reaction.

Must every reaction disappear within 48 hours?

No. Most settle within a few days, commonly one to three days. Worsening or persistent symptoms, poor drinking, breathing changes or unusual drowsiness need advice rather than waiting for a deadline.

Should I give pain medicine before the injection?

Routine medicine solely to prevent vaccine symptoms is generally not recommended. If the child is uncomfortable afterwards, ask about an appropriate product and weight-based dose. Do not stop an existing prescribed medicine without advice.

Does having no fever mean the vaccine did not work?

No. The presence or absence of short-term symptoms is not a reliable measure of protection.

Which symptoms might suggest myocarditis?

New chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations need urgent assessment. Young children can show rapid breathing, unusual lethargy, poor feeding or vomiting. Severe symptoms or collapse require emergency care.

Is heart inflammation risk the same for every child?

No. It varies with age, sex, product, dose and interval. A rate from an older formulation or a broad age group is not an exact estimate for an individual child.

Can children younger than 12 receive a vaccine?

Current programmes include younger children, but the product, eligibility and schedule depend on the country and the child’s circumstances. US and Canadian guidance includes consideration from six months; ask the local service for the current recommendation.

Why consider vaccination if most children have mild COVID-19?

Some children develop serious illness, and certain health conditions increase risk. The expected benefit and the uncommon risks should be discussed for that child rather than assuming either zero disease risk or identical benefit for everyone.

Can my child receive another dose after myocarditis?

This needs specialist advice. When myocarditis or pericarditis developed within three weeks of a COVID-19 vaccine, CDC generally advises avoiding another dose unless an individual assessment supports it after recovery.

Should we report a suspected reaction even if the cause is uncertain?

Yes. The clinician or local reporting system can record and investigate important suspected reactions. Reporting helps surveillance; it does not by itself prove that vaccination caused the event.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
